title: Dimension-Free Multimodal Sampling via Preconditioned Annealed Langevin Dynamics
one_liner: Preconditioned annealed Langevin dynamics keeps sampling quality stable as the problem grows to higher dimensions by rescaling which weights matter.
lead: To sample from a function with multiple peaks, algorithms like annealed Langevin dynamics gradually smooth out the peaks into a single hill, then slowly sharpen it back up to find all the original peaks. But as the problem grows bigger (more dimensions), errors tend to pile up and destroy the solution. This paper proves you can prevent that pileup by preconditioning: rescaling the smoothing to match the problem's natural shape.

problem.h2: Sampling gets noisier in high dimensions
paras: Imagine you want to sample random points from a function with multiple peaks. A naive approach: take random steps with noise added each time, always sliding downhill when you go uphill. That works in 2D. But in 100D, the randomness gets so large that your sampler never settles into the quiet valleys between peaks.

Annealed Langevin dynamics is a smarter walk: first you mathematically blur all the peaks together into one smooth hill, then slowly sharpen the hill back up as you take steps. That forces the walker to explore all the original peak locations. But theory offers no guarantee it stays accurate as the problem grows to 1000D, 10000D. Mistakes pile up invisibly across all those dimensions.

callout.html: This paper proves that rescaling the smoothing to match the problem's local shape stops errors from piling up across dimensions.

steps.text: Link how smooth the function becomes to its actual bumpy structure.
Gradually reduce smoothing in a predictable way over time.
Build a rescaling matrix whose spectrum (the list of how strong each rescaling is) decays fast enough.
Show that under these conditions, mistakes do not accumulate as dimensions grow.
Prove the method still works if your estimate of which way is uphill is a bit wrong.

paras: Annealed Langevin dynamics already exists. The paper modifies it by adding a preconditioner: a rescaling operator that adjusts how strongly each coordinate responds to the smoothing. This prevents errors from accumulating along coordinates with large curvature.
object.object: Preconditioner operator in annealed Langevin dynamics

hidden.h2: Spectral decay: measuring how fast errors vanish
hidden.name: Spectrum decay rate of the preconditioner
paras: The hidden quantity is the spectrum of the preconditioner: a list of strengths (called eigenvalues), one for each direction in the function. A fast-decaying spectrum means the first few directions are strongly rescaled, while later directions get weak rescaling.

The paper measures this by checking: does the preconditioner's spectrum decay fast enough that when you add up all the errors across directions, they do not blow up? If yes, dimension-uniform stability holds.

heat.caption: Darker directions get stronger rescaling. Fast decay means only early dimensions need help.

reads.html: The preconditioner is like a volume knob that turns down differently on each radio channel. Some channels (important directions) get full volume, others (less important) get quiet. If the volume decay is steep enough, no single channel ever gets so loud that it breaks the speaker.
The spectrum of the preconditioner must decay sufficiently fast (e.g., exponentially) so that coordinate-wise error accumulation is controlled by a finite constant independent of problem dimension.

mechanism.h2: Why rescaling by spectrum prevents error accumulation
paras: Errors in a random walk grow like the square root of time. In D dimensions, you have D independent sources of error. Without correction, they add up: total error scales like sqrt(D times each error). That is why naive algorithms fail in high dimensions.

Annealing helps because it merges all peaks into a single smooth hill early on, so the walker cannot get stuck in a single valley—then as smoothing is gradually removed, the walker naturally spreads across all the true peaks. But if the function is bumpy in some directions and smooth in others, the bumpy directions still accumulate errors as you add more dimensions. Preconditioning fixes this by rescaling: strong rescaling on bumpy directions holds the walker steady there (since those directions are naturally noisy), weak rescaling on smooth directions lets it move freely. The key is spectral decay: if rescaling gets weaker fast enough (exponentially), then the total error across all dimensions stays bounded by a constant, independent of D, because the sum of all mistakes follows a convergent series that never exceeds a limit.

stages.s: Function with multiple peaks plus imperfect directional guesses
Smooth the function with a covariance matrix, making all peaks merge
Apply preconditioner: rescale each dimension by its spectrum value
Run annealed Langevin walk on the rescaled, smoothed function
Gradually unsmoosh: reduce smoothing while keeping rescaling active
Accurate samples from all peaks, error bounded independent of dimension

math.h2: The key equation and worked example
math.words: Error-bound equation: total-error grows like sum-over-dimensions of (spectral-weight-i times coordinate-error-i), but if weights decay exponentially, the sum stays finite.
symbols: A constant independent of D (the number of dimensions)
The i-th spectral weight (strength of rescaling in direction i)
The error in direction i (grows as sqrt(time / dimension))
Number of dimensions in the problem

worked.title: A tiny worked example with 6 dimensions
lines: Suppose each direction has baseline error e_i = 0.1.
Without preconditioner, all lambda_i = 1, so total error = 1.0 * 0.1 * 6 = 0.6.
With preconditioner using exponential decay lambda_i = 2^(-i): lambda_1=1.0, lambda_2=0.5, lambda_3=0.25, lambda_4=0.125, lambda_5=0.0625, lambda_6=0.03125.
The sum converges even if you added more dimensions: adding dimension 7 with lambda_7=0.0156 adds only 0.00156 to the total.
Result: preconditioner shrinks error by 3x while keeping the error bounded as D grows.

math.note: Fast spectral decay means a finite sum of weighted errors replaces an unbounded accumulation.

charts.note: Errors accumulate; quality collapses in high dimensions.

charts.title: Annealed Langevin without preconditioning
charts.note: Annealing helps the walker explore all peaks, but errors still grow with dimension because mistakes from each coordinate accumulate into a larger total without spectral decay to slow that accumulation.

charts.title: Preconditioned annealed Langevin
charts.note: Spectral decay holds error stable across all dimensions.

items.b: Spectrum does not decay fast enough.
items.html: If the preconditioner's spectrum decays slowly (e.g., polynomially instead of exponentially), errors still accumulate as D grows. The method requires fast decay.
The paper assumes errors in your uphill-direction guesses are small and random. If your score model is systematically wrong (always too steep or always too shallow), preconditioning cannot fix that.

items.b: Smoothing covariance and preconditioner are mismatched.
items.html: The spectral condition links the smoothing matrix to how bumpy the function is. If you choose them independently, you lose the dimension-uniform guarantee.

If the preconditioner spectrum decays fast, the smoothing covariance is well-tuned to the target, and scores are roughly accurate, the method samples from all peaks with bounded error regardless of dimension.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 2D target: two bell-shaped peaks far apart, then embed it in 10D, 100D, 1000D by repeating the pattern in higher coordinates. Sample from each version using: (1) naive Langevin, (2) annealed Langevin alone, (3) preconditioned annealed Langevin with exponentially decaying spectrum. Measure the divergence (a mismatch score between the samples you drew and the true target bell-curves) for each method at each dimension. Plot it.
demo.metric_eq: divergence = sum_{peaks} (sample-density at peak - true-density at peak) / true-density
demo.closing: The preconditioned method's KL should stay roughly flat across dimensions, while the others climb steeply.
